title: Average surprise
objectives: Compute the entropy of a distribution and find when it is largest.

screens.prose: Two coins. One is fair. The other lands heads 90% of the time. For the bent coin, heads carries $-\log_2 0.9 = 0.152$ bits and tails $-\log_2 0.1 = 3.322$ bits.
screens.question: Over many tosses of the bent coin, how many bits does one toss carry on average? Give a decimal to 3 places.

hints.text: An average over many tosses weighs each outcome by its chance.
Heads: chance 0.9, surprise 0.152. Tails: chance 0.1, surprise 3.322.
Work out $0.9 \times 0.152 + 0.1 \times 3.322$.

feedback.correct: Weigh each surprise by how often it happens: 0.469 bits a toss.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Heads happens 90% of the time, so its surprise counts nine times as often.

byKey.unweighted: You averaged the two surprises equally. Heads comes up nine times as often as tails.
byKey.summed: You added the two surprises. Each toss gives one of them, so weigh them by their chances.
byKey.heads-only: That is heads alone. Tails happens 10% of the time and carries 3.322 bits.

explain.text: $0.9 \times 0.152 + 0.1 \times 3.322 = 0.137 + 0.332 = 0.469$ bits. This is the expected value of the surprise, as in a long-run average.

screens.prose: The curve gives the average surprise of a coin whose heads chance is $p$. Drag the point from the bent coin at 0.9 to other coins.

options.text: At $p = 0.5$, where the curve reaches 1 bit
At $p = 0.9$, because tails then carries 3.3 bits
options.why: Tails is surprising there, but it is rare. The average at 0.9 is only 0.469 bits.

options.text: Near $p = 0$ and $p = 1$, where outcomes are rarest
options.why: Near the ends one outcome is almost sure, so the average falls towards 0.
The curve is not flat. The bent coin carried 0.469 bits.

feedback.correct: The fair coin is the hardest to predict: 1 bit a toss.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Drag the point and read where the curve peaks.

explain.text: The curve peaks at $p = 0.5$ with 1 bit and falls to 0 at both ends. A coin that nearly always lands one way tells us little each toss.

screens.prose: The average surprise is the **entropy**: $H = \sum_i p_i(-\log_2 p_i)$, the expected value of the surprise. A weather station reports four states with chances $\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18$.
screens.question: What is the entropy of the weather, in bits?

hints.text: The surprises are $-\log_2$ of each chance: 1, 2, 3, 3.
Multiply each by its chance.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply each surprise by its chance, then add.

byKey.unweighted: You averaged the surprises 1, 2, 3, 3 equally. Weigh each by its chance.
byKey.summed: You added the four surprises. Each report gives one of them: weigh by chance.
byKey.count: That is $\log_2 4$, which assumes four equal chances. These chances differ.

explain.text: The surprises are 1, 2, 3 and 3 bits. Weighted by chance: $\tfrac12 \cdot 1 + \tfrac14 \cdot 2 + \tfrac18 \cdot 3 + \tfrac18 \cdot 3 = 1.75$ bits.

screens.prose: Another station has four states with equal chances, $\tfrac14$ each.
screens.question: What is its entropy, in bits?

hints.text: Every state has the same surprise.
$-\log_2 \tfrac14 = 2$.
An average of four 2s is 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Each state has surprise 2 bits; weigh by chance and add.

byKey.one-term: That is one term, $\tfrac14 \times 2$. There are four states.
byKey.summed: You added the four surprises without their chances.
byKey.chance: That is one chance. The entropy is the average surprise.

explain.text: Each state carries $-\log_2 \tfrac14 = 2$ bits, so the average is 2 bits. Equal chances give $\log_2 n$: here more than the 1.75 of the uneven station.

screens.prose: A third station has chances 0.4, 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1. The table gives each surprise and two of the four terms $p \times (-\log_2 p)$.
screens.question: Fill in the two missing terms and the total, to 3 places.

hints.text: Each term is $p$ times its surprise.
Row two: $0.3 \times 1.737$. Row four: $0.1 \times 3.322$.
Add all four terms for the total.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Each term is the chance times its surprise; the total adds the four terms.

byKey.no-weight: You copied the surprise. The term is $0.3 \times 1.737$.
byKey.unweighted: You averaged the four surprises equally. Add the weighted terms instead.

explain.text: $0.3 \times 1.737 = 0.521$ and $0.1 \times 3.322 = 0.332$. The total is 1.846 bits: between the 1.75 and the 2 of the last two stations.

screens.prose: Four ways to share chance among four states. Step through them with the control.
screens.question: Which one has the largest entropy?

options.why: A is dominated by one state, so most reports are expected. Its entropy is 1.357 bits.
B is the weather station of 1.75 bits. D is flatter.
C is close to flat, with 1.846 bits, but D is flatter still.

hints.text: Recall the coin: the curve peaked where both sides were equal.
The flatter the chances, the less you can predict.
Pick the share with all four chances equal.

feedback.correct: Equal chances give the most: $\log_2 4 = 2$ bits.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which one is flattest?

explain.text: A to D carry 1.357, 1.75, 1.846 and 2 bits. For $n$ outcomes the entropy is at most $\log_2 n$, reached only at equal chances; level 2 proves it with Jensen.

screens.prose: A colleague says a die with 100 faces must have more entropy than a coin. This die is loaded so hard that it shows 1 every time.
screens.question: What is its entropy?

options.why: That is $\log_2 100$, the most 100 faces can carry. It needs equal chances, and these are 1 and 0.
A coin with equal chances carries 1 bit. This die has no doubt at all.
Entropy counts bits of doubt, not faces.

hints.text: What do you learn when the die lands?
Face 1 has chance 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Every roll shows 1. How surprised are we?

byKey.log100: You counted the faces. Entropy depends on the chances, and here one face takes them all.
byKey.hundred: You counted faces as bits. Count doubt instead.

explain.text: The only outcome has chance 1 and surprise 0; the other faces have chance 0 and add nothing. The number of outcomes sets the most entropy can be, not what it is.

screens.prose: A coin has chances $\tfrac12, \tfrac12$ and a third outcome, landing on its edge, with chance 0. The term $-p\log_2 p$ is drawn below: it shrinks to 0 as $p$ does.
screens.question: What is the entropy of the three outcomes?

options.why: That is $\log_2 3$, three equal chances. The edge has chance 0, so it adds nothing.
The term is $p\log_2 p$, not $\log_2 p$ alone, and it tends to 0. Read the curve near $p = 0$.
Each half carries 1 bit and is weighted by $\tfrac12$: the two terms add to 1.

hints.text: Split it into three terms $-p\log_2 p$.
The curve shows the term at $p = 0$ is 0.
Each half gives $\tfrac12 \times 1$.

feedback.correct: The two halves give 1 bit; the edge adds 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out each term $-p\log_2 p$.

byKey.undefined: You stopped at $\log_2 0$. The term multiplies it by $p = 0$, and the product tends to 0.

explain.text: $-p\log_2 p \to 0$ as $p \to 0$, so we take a term with $p = 0$ as 0. The entropy is $\tfrac12 + \tfrac12 + 0 = 1$ bit.

screens.prose: Every time, you weighed each surprise by its chance and added. $$H = \sum_i p_i(-\log_2 p_i) = E[-\log_2 p(X)],$$ with terms where $p_i = 0$ left out. For $n$ outcomes, $0 \le H \le \log_2 n$; the top is reached at equal chances.
screens.question: A signal is long, flat or short with chances $\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac14$. What is its entropy?

options.why: That is $\log_2 3$, for three equal chances. These are not equal.
You averaged the surprises 1, 2, 2 equally. Weigh them by chance.
You added the surprises. Weigh each by its chance.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Weigh each surprise by its chance.

explain.text: Surprises 1, 2 and 2 bits, weighted by $\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac14$, give 1.5 bits: below the $\log_2 3 \approx 1.585$ of three equal chances.

screens.prose: Now in Python. A distribution is a list of chances that add to 1. Leave out the zero chances: `math.log2(0)` raises an error.
screens.question: Complete `entropy_bits(probs)`.

widget.starter:
import math

def entropy_bits(probs):
    """The entropy of a distribution, in bits. Chances of 0 add nothing."""
    ...
widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests. Each value is accepted within 1e-9 of the exact entropy.

hints.text: Each term is `p * math.log2(p)`, with a minus sign in front of the sum.
Use a generator inside `sum`.
Add `if p > 0` so zero chances are skipped.

feedback.correct: Your function adds $-p\log_2 p$ over the chances above 0.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Read the first failing row.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. A chance of 0 inside `math.log2` raises one: skip those terms.

explain.text:
One line does it. The `if p > 0` filter is the rule that a zero chance adds nothing.

```python
return -sum(p * math.log2(p) for p in probs if p > 0)
```

screens.prose: A strategy sends one signal a day: long with chance 0.6, flat 0.3, short 0.1. A signal that is always long tells us nothing new each day.
screens.question: How many bits a day does this signal carry? Give a decimal to 3 places.

hints.text: The surprises are $-\log_2 0.6$, $-\log_2 0.3$ and $-\log_2 0.1$.
They are 0.737, 1.737 and 3.322 bits.
Weigh by 0.6, 0.3 and 0.1 and add.

feedback.correct: About 1.295 bits a day: less than the 1.585 of three equal chances.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out $\sum p(-\log_2 p)$ over the three signals.

byKey.equal: That is $\log_2 3$, for equal chances. Long comes up 60% of the time.
byKey.nats: You used ln: 0.898 nats. Divide by $\ln 2$.
byKey.log10: You used base 10. Bits need base 2.

explain.text: $0.6 \times 0.737 + 0.3 \times 1.737 + 0.1 \times 3.322 = 0.442 + 0.521 + 0.332 = 1.295$ bits. An always-long signal has 0 bits; one long or short half the time has 1.

ideas: Entropy is the average surprise: each outcome's $-\log_2 p$ weighed by its chance $p$.
For $n$ outcomes it lies between 0 (one sure outcome) and $\log_2 n$ (equal chances).
Outcomes of chance 0 add nothing, because $p\log_2 p \to 0$ as $p \to 0$.

formula.name: Entropy
formula.note: In bits; the sum runs over outcomes with $p_i > 0$.

summary.trap: Reading entropy off the number of outcomes: a 100-faced die that always shows 1 has entropy 0.

quiz.prose: Signal A is a fair coin. Signal B has three values with chances 0.98, 0.01 and 0.01.
quiz.question: Which has more entropy?

options.text: B, because it has more values
options.why: More values raise only the ceiling, $\log_2 3$. B is almost always the same value.
They differ: 1 bit against about 0.161 bits.

feedback.correct: A carries 1 bit; B only about 0.161.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out B: one value has chance 0.98.

explain.text: B: $0.98 \times 0.029 + 2 \times 0.01 \times 6.644 \approx 0.161$ bits, well under A's 1 bit. The count of values is not the entropy.

quiz.prose: A forecast can say one of five things.
quiz.question: What is the most entropy it can have, in bits? Give a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.correct: The most is $\log_2 5 \approx 2.322$ bits, at equal chances.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The largest entropy comes with equal chances.
